entities.summary:
The Siege of Carthage was a pivotal 17-year conflict between the Roman Republic and Carthage, a major power in the ancient Mediterranean. It began in 149 BCE and ended in 146 BCE, with the Romans ultimately capturing and destroying the city. This devastating outcome marked the end of Punic power and had far-reaching consequences for the region.

The siege was a brutal and drawn-out struggle, with both sides suffering heavy losses. The Romans, led by Scipio Aemilianus, employed innovative tactics and besieged the city from both land and sea. The Carthaginians, led by Hasdrubal the Boeotarch, fought valiantly but were ultimately unable to withstand the Roman onslaught.

The fall of Carthage sent shockwaves throughout the ancient world, leading to the rise of Rome as the dominant power in the Mediterranean. It also marked the beginning of the Roman era of expansion and conquest, which would shape the course of Western civilization for centuries to come.

The siege's legacy can be seen in the enduring rivalry between Rome and Carthage, with echoes of their conflict still resonating in modern geopolitics. As the renowned historian Polybius noted, 'The war between Rome and Carthage was the greatest and most memorable conflict of the ancient world.'
